newsitem.title: UK: Pollution may cause heart attacks, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Pollution may cause heart attacks, study finds.

text.p: Up to one in 50 heart attacks treated at London hospitals may be caused by air pollution, British researchers reported on Tuesday.
They said levels of black smoke, nitric oxide, carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxode were all linked with heart attack.
Writing in the journal Occupational and Environmental Medicine, Jan Polniecki of London's St George's Hospital Medical School and colleagues said there were other heath effects, too.
Nitric oxide was linked with irregular heart rhythms, black smoke with chest pain and carbon monoxide with other circulatory diseases.
"No association was found between ozone and circulatory diseases," they added.
Polniecki's team measured levels of the chemical pollutants and cross-checked them against data on heart attacks and other heart complaints.
They found significant associations with heart attack, but only in the "cool season," they wrote.

"Biologically plausible mechanisms have been advanced by which emissions, mainly from motor vehicles, might trigger circulatory disorders," they wrote. This could include inflammation of the airways, they added.
"Our results strengthen the case for the existence of a causal link with myocardial infarction (heart attack)."
They said more research, involving more people, was needed.
